title: 4Sum II
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every combination directly versus meet in the middle with a hash map.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given four integer arrays nums1, nums2, nums3, and nums4, all of the same length n, count how many tuples (i, j, k, l) exist such that nums1[i] plus nums2[j] plus nums3[k] plus nums4[l] equals 0.

blocks.caption: Precompute one half's sums into a hash map, then look up the negated sum for the other half

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A sum of 4 independent choices must equal a target (0)","Split into two independent halves: precompute one half's sums, look up the complement in the other"],["n to the 4th power combinations directly is too slow","Meet in the middle: reduces n to the 4th power down to roughly two passes of n squared"],["Need to count how many pairs produce a given sum, not just whether one exists","A hash map storing sum to frequency, not just a hash set of sums"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given four integer arrays nums1, nums2, nums3, and nums4, all of the same length n, count how many tuples (i, j, k, l) exist such that nums1[i] plus nums2[j] plus nums3[k] plus nums4[l] equals 0.

blocks.title: Analogy: Balancing a Four Way Financial Ledger to Zero
blocks.text: Like picking one transaction from each of four separate ledgers and counting every possible combination of the four that together balance out to exactly zero.

blocks.caption: Count every combination of one index from each of the four arrays whose values sum to zero

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples

blocks.content: {"headers":["Combination","Sum","Why"],"rows":[["1 (index 0) plus (-2) (index 0) plus (-1) (index 0) plus 2 (index 1)","sum equals 0","1 plus (-2) plus (-1) plus 2 equals 0, one valid combination taking specific indices from all four arrays"],["2 (index 1) plus (-1) (index 1) plus (-1) (index 0) plus 0 (index 0)","sum equals 0","2 plus (-1) plus (-1) plus 0 equals 0, a second, independent valid combination using a different set of indices"]]}

blocks.text: Example: nums1 = [0], nums2 = [0], nums3 = [0], nums4 = [0]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The only possible combination is 0 + 0 + 0 + 0","equals 0","With only one element in each array, exactly one combination exists at all, and it happens to sum to 0"],["Answer","1","There is exactly one valid tuple, since only one combination is even possible"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: arrays with no combination summing to zero at all
If no combination of one value from each array ever adds up to 0, the answer is simply 0.
5. How Should We Think?

Before checking every one of the n to the 4th power combinations, notice this problem is really just an extended Two Sum: instead of 2 arrays summing to a target, it is 4 arrays summing to 0, and 4 things summing to 0 can always be split into two pairs that must sum to opposites of each other.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: nums1[i] plus nums2[j] plus nums3[k] plus nums4[l] equals 0 can be rearranged as (nums1[i] plus nums2[j]) equals the negation of (nums3[k] plus nums4[l]), splitting the 4-way sum into two independent 2-way sums that must be exact negations of each other.

Observation 2: Once split this way, every possible sum from the first two arrays can be precomputed once, and counted, using a hash map, since there are only n squared such pairs, not n to the 4th power full combinations.

Observation 3: For every pair from the last two arrays, the exact count of first-half pairs that would complete a sum of 0 is just a single hash map lookup for the negated sum, an O(1) operation instead of a nested search.

Observation 4: Because the hash map stores counts, not just presence, a single lookup directly returns how many valid combinations that specific second-half pair contributes, without needing to enumerate them individually.

Whenever a "k things must sum to a target" problem's k is larger than 2, look for a natural way to split it into two independent halves, precompute one half's sums into a frequency map, and look up the complement for the other half.

This is the classic "meet in the middle" technique: instead of searching one giant combined space of size n to the 4th power, two much smaller spaces of size n squared each are searched independently and joined by a single hash map lookup.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every possible combination of one index from each of the four arrays directly, summing their values and counting how many combinations equal 0.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every combination of indices i, j, k, l (one from each array), compute the sum of the four values.
If the sum equals 0, increment the count.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: All four loops range over the exact same length n, since the problem guarantees all four arrays are the same size, letting a single n be reused for every loop bound.
count is only incremented, never reset, across the entire quadruple-nested loop, since every one of the n to the 4th power combinations is an independent, equally valid candidate to check.
The sum of all four selected values is computed fresh for every combination, since there is no shared partial sum yet being reused between combinations at this stage.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every combination of one index from each array is directly checked, so the true count is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n to the 4th power), checking every combination of four indices.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.

Limitation: the problem naturally splits into two independent halves. Precomputing every possible sum from the first two arrays once means the last two arrays only need to look up a target value, instead of trying every combination of all four together.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Checking every one of the n to the 4th power combinations wastes an enormous amount of repeated work, since the same nums1[i] plus nums2[j] partial sum gets recomputed inside the innermost two loops for every single choice of k and l, even though it never actually depends on k or l at all. If that partial sum is instead computed once for every (i, j) pair, up front, and tallied by value into a hash map, then the remaining question for every (k, l) pair becomes purely a lookup: how many times has the value that would cancel nums3[k] plus nums4[l] down to 0 already been seen? That lookup costs O(1), collapsing what was an O(n squared) inner search, over k and l, for every i and j, down to a single hash map access, cutting the total complexity from O(n to the 4th power) to O(n squared).

Compute every possible sum of one value from nums1 and one from nums2, and count how many times each such sum occurs using a hash map. Then, for every combination of one value from nums3 and one from nums4, compute their sum and look up how many pairs from nums1 and nums2 summed to exactly the negation of that value, adding that count to the running total.
9. Optimized Solution
Precompute all pairwise sums of the first two arrays into a hash map, then look up the negated sum for every pair of the last two arrays.
Dry run for nums1 = [1, 2], nums2 = [-2, -1], nums3 = [-1, 2], nums4 = [0, 2]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["All sums of nums1 plus nums2: 1-2=-1, 1-1=0, 2-2=0, 2-1=1","sum counts: -1:1, 0:2, 1:1","Every one of the 4 possible pairs from nums1 and nums2 contributes its sum to the tally, with 0 appearing twice since two different pairs both produce it"],["For each pair of nums3 and nums4, look up the negation of their sum","-1+0=-1, need sum 1: count 1. -1+2=1, need sum -1: count 1. 2+0=2, need sum -2: count 0. 2+2=4, need sum -4: count 0","Each pair needs a first-half sum of exactly the negation of its own sum to bring the total to 0, so the map is queried at that specific negated value"],["Total","1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 2","Summing every pair's individual lookup result gives the overall count of tuples summing to 0"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: precompute pairwise sums of the first two arrays, look up the negated sum for the last two

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for building the sum map and for the lookup pass.
Space: O(n squared), for the map of pairwise sums in the worst case.
Why This Works

sum_counts[s] correctly stores exactly how many pairs from nums1 and nums2 produce the sum s, since every such pair is tallied once during the first double loop. For a given pair from nums3 and nums4, looking up the negation of their sum is therefore exactly the number of first-half pairs that, combined with this specific second-half pair, bring the total four-way sum to exactly 0, since two sums add to 0 exactly when one equals the negation of the other. Summing this lookup result over every second-half pair therefore counts every valid 4-tuple exactly once, with no combination missed or double-counted.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quantity","Meaning"],"rows":[["sum_counts[s]","The number of pairs from nums1 and nums2 whose values sum to exactly s"],["sum_counts at the negation of a given pair's sum","The number of first-half pairs that, together with this pair, complete a 4-way sum of exactly 0"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The first double loop over nums1 and nums2 runs to completion before the second double loop begins, since every possible first-half sum must be tallied before any lookup against it can be trusted as complete.
The map update safely increments a sum's tally whether or not that exact sum has been seen before.
The second double loop computes the lookup target as the negation of the current pair's sum, directly reflecting the rearranged equation that the whole optimization is built on.

count is incremented by the full lookup result, not just by 1, since a single second-half pair can complete a 0-sum with every one of potentially several different first-half pairs that share the same needed sum.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (check every combination)","O(n to the 4th power)","O(1)","Every one of the n to the 4th power possible tuples is directly checked and summed"],["Optimized (meet in the middle with a hash map)","O(n squared)","O(n squared)","Two independent O(n squared) passes, joined by O(1) average hash map lookups"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Splitting a "sum of k things equals a target" problem into two independent halves, precomputing all sums of one half into a hash map, and looking up the complement for the other half, is the standard meet in the middle technique for extending two-sum style problems to more arrays.
Common mistakes

items: Splitting the four arrays unevenly or incorrectly, instead of exactly two and two, which is what allows both halves to be reduced to O(n squared) work each; an uneven split would leave one half still needing a much larger computation.
Forgetting the negation when looking up the target sum, since the goal is for the two halves to sum to 0 together, not to match each other directly, a subtle but critical sign error.

Using a hash set of sums instead of a hash map of sum counts, which would only answer "does at least one pair produce this sum" instead of "how many pairs produce this sum", undercounting whenever multiple pairs share a sum.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["All arrays containing only zeros","Every combination sums to zero, and the sum count map correctly reflects that with a single key holding a count of n squared"],["No combination summing to zero at all","The final count correctly stays 0, since every lookup against the sum map returns 0"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly name this as "meet in the middle", since recognizing that a 4 array sum problem is just two independent 2 array sum problems joined by a hash map lookup is the entire insight needed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "k arrays or groups must combine to a target sum, where k is greater than 2" points toward meet in the middle: split into two halves, precompute one half's combined sums into a frequency map, then look up the needed complement for the other half.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this generalize to 6 arrays instead of 4? Split into two groups of 3 arrays each, precompute all sums from one group into a hash map, and look up the negated sum for every combination in the other group, replacing an even larger combination count with two much smaller ones.

What if the target were a nonzero value instead of 0? The same technique applies directly; the lookup value simply becomes the target minus the second half's sum instead of just the negation of the second half's sum.

How would you also return the actual tuples, not just their count? Instead of counting occurrences, store a list of index pairs per sum in the map, then for every second-half pair, retrieve and combine with the matching list of first-half pairs.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Direct extension of the classic Two Sum hash map technique, applied here across two independently precomputed halves instead of one single array.
Same "split into two independent halves, meet with a hash map" meet-in-the-middle idea used in subset-sum style problems where the full search space would otherwise be exponential.
Same "store counts, not just presence, in the hash map" requirement as any problem that must count occurrences rather than just detect existence.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n to the 4th power) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (meet in the middle with a hash map): O(n squared) time, O(n squared) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Meet in the middle, splitting a 4-way sum into two independent 2-way sums joined by a hash map
Core Idea: Precompute every possible sum of the first two arrays into a frequency map, then for every pair of the last two arrays, look up how many first-half pairs would complete a sum of exactly 0
Time: O(n squared)
Space: O(n squared), for the map of pairwise sums

Most Important Observation: A sum-to-target problem over more than 2 groups can often be split into two independently precomputable halves joined by one hash map lookup, turning a high power of n into roughly its square root power
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Split in half, tally one side, look up the negation on the other
